chunks: My father, may Allah grant him mercy, said: We were told by Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from his father, from Abbas ibn Amr al-Fuqaymi, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said to the heretic - when he asked him about Allah, what is He? -
He said: He is a Thing different to all things. Return my saying 'a thing' to confirming a meaning, and that He is a Thing by the truth of Thingness, except that He is not a body nor an image.

key_terms.بِخِلَافِ الْأَشْيَاءِ: Different from other things; indicating unique distinction from creation.
key_terms.جَسَد: Body; physical substance, which Allah lacks.
key_terms.حَقِيقَةُ الشَّيْئِيَّةِ: The truth/reality of Thingness; affirming the core attribute of being an entity.
key_terms.شَيْءٌ: A thing/entity; used here to affirm Allah's existence and reality.
key_terms.صُورَةٌ: Image/Form; visible shape or figure, which Allah lacks.

ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology define Allah as a 'Thing' while remaining distinct from physical creation?
ai.summary: In this foundational hadith from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) articulates the Shia doctrine of *Tawhid al-Sifat* by affirming Allah as a 'Thing' (*Shay'*) to establish His real existence, while negating physical attributes like body (*Jasad*) and form (*Surah*) to prevent anthropomorphism. This definition serves as a critical theological boundary against the *Zanadiqa* (gnostics/heretics) of the era, distinguishing divine essence from created matter without falling into the extreme negation of attributes. The narration underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on affirming divine reality through linguistic convention while maintaining absolute transcendence.
